# Results — Study 678 (Random-Walk-Index)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — Michael
Poulos' **Random Walk Index**: a market that has moved farther over the last *n* sessions than a
random walk of the same Average True Range would be expected to move is "statistically
non-random," and **RWI-high > 1** is the mechanical trigger to ride the trend. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of
**2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped).
Fingerprints `98e6db1a1e26` (SPY) / `70e1bc4a725e` (QQQ) / `7c02d693031f` (IWM) /
`f1faf16222de` (DIA) / `a0f0673984c4` (GLD).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily total-return-adjusted OHLC (`auto_adjust=True` — Open/High/Low/Close all scaled together so splits/dividends never fake a giant range on the bar), SPY + basket (QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD), 5,406 rows each, 2005-01-03 → 2026-06-30 |
| Indicator | RWI-high(n) = (High_t − Low_{t−n}) / (ATR_n(t) × √n), simple (non-Wilder) ATR; the reported RWI-high is the **max over n = 2..6** (Poulos' own short-lookback scan) |
| Flag | RWI-high(t) **> 1** — the textbook "statistically non-random uptrend, ride it" trigger |
| Statistics | Welch *t* for the flag/no-flag split (daily, effectively non-overlapping observations); **Newey-West (5 lags)** *t* on the flag-dummy regression; Wilson interval on the hit rate; a 20-seed × 1,000-draw matched-count random-day placebo; a 20-seed **block-shuffled** (21-day blocks) random-entry control for the tradable book |
| Execution / costs | one documented convention: the flag is computed from data through the close of day *t* (it needs that day's own High/Low), entered **at that same close**, and earns the close(t) → close(t+1) return — a single shift, applied once. Costs one-way × NAV per leg on every position change (5 / 10 bps) |
| Survivorship | none named — SPY/QQQ/IWM/DIA are indices/index ETFs, GLD tracks a physical commodity; no cross-sectional membership panel is used anywhere in this study |

## The headline (SPY) — RWI-high flag day vs no-flag day, next-session return

| quantity | flag day (RWI-high > 1) | no-flag day |
|---|--:|--:|
| n | **3,067** | 2,336 |
| mean next-session return | **+2.41 bps** | +8.07 bps |
| gap | **−5.66 bps** | |
| Welch *t* | **−1.64** | |
| Newey-West *t* (5 lags) | **−1.74** | |
| hit rate (next-session return > 0) | **55.1%** (Wilson 95% [53.4%, 56.9%]) | |

The flag fires on **56.8%** of SPY sessions since 2005 — already a warning sign for a threshold
billed as detecting a "statistically non-random" event: taking the max of five overlapping
lookback statistics (n = 2..6) inflates the false-positive rate of a raw "> 1" cutoff badly. And
the direction is **backwards**: flagged sessions are followed by a *smaller* average return than
unflagged ones, not a larger one. On SPY alone the gap doesn't clear the ±2 bar (*t* = −1.64), but
it already leans the wrong way.

**Matched-count random-day placebo:** observed flag-day mean +2.41 bps vs a placebo mean of
+4.85 bps (sd 1.41 bps) over **20,000 draws** (20 seeds × 1,000) of a random 3,067-session
subset → **p = 0.9591** — a random subset of the same size does *better* than the RWI flag
96% of the time. The flag is not just failing to add value; it is picking a below-average subset
of days.

## Cross-instrument — SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD (2005-01 → 2026-06)

| ticker | n flag | flag bps | rest bps | gap bps | Welch *t* | NW *t* | hit % |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 3,067 | +2.41 | +8.07 | −5.66 | −1.64 | −1.74 | 55.1% |
| QQQ | 3,013 | +4.98 | +8.84 | −3.86 | −0.99 | −1.06 | 55.9% |
| IWM | 2,783 | +1.06 | +8.40 | −7.34 | −1.76 | −1.82 | 52.4% |
| DIA | 2,955 | +3.84 | +5.25 | −1.41 | −0.44 | −0.47 | 55.4% |
| GLD | 2,771 | +5.04 | +4.24 | +0.80 | +0.26 | +0.27 | 52.4% |
| **pooled** (n = 27,015) | | **+3.47** | **+6.92** | **−3.45** | **−2.16** | | |

Four of five names show a negative gap; the pooled Welch *t* = **−2.16** *clears* the desk's
±2 bar — but in the **wrong direction**. Read honestly: this is not "no effect," it is a small,
statistically real *headwind*: flagging a session as "non-random trend" mechanically selects for
days that pay *less* than average over the next session, not more. Consistent with the mean
reversion that shows up after any sharp, ATR-scaled short-term price burst.

## The long timer, as an actual book (SPY, one-day execution lag)

| | total return, 2005→2026 | Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|
| RWI-high long timer, **gross** | +81.76% | +0.301 |
| RWI-high long timer, **net 5 bps** | **+0.55%** | **+0.060** |
| RWI-high long timer, **net 10 bps** | −44.39% | −0.181 |
| **Buy & hold SPY** | **+831.34%** | **+0.644** |

Exposure: **56.8%** of sessions invested, **1,184** position changes over 21.5 years
(~2.76%/yr in turnover cost at 5 bps one-way). Even **before** costs, the timer captures barely a
tenth of buy & hold's total return over the same window and roughly half its Sharpe; realistic
costs (5–10 bps one-way) push net performance to flat-to-negative. Being long a "statistically
non-random uptrend" 57% of the time, on the tape that actually happened, is *not* a free way to
outrun the index.

## The fair control — block-shuffled random entry, same exposure & turnover texture

The flag series is chopped into 21-day blocks and the block order is randomly permuted (20
seeds) — this preserves the timer's total days-invested count *and* its turnover/run-length
profile while destroying any real correlation between "the flag fired here" and what actually
happened at that calendar date. This is the fair, exposure- and cost-matched benchmark the claim
has to beat, not a naive buy & hold race.

| | value |
|---|--:|
| random-entry control, mean total return (20 seeds) | **+98.60%** (sd 58.86) |
| random-entry control, mean Sharpe (20 seeds) | **+0.280** (sd 0.105) |
| RWI timer, net 5 bps | +0.55% total return, +0.060 Sharpe |
| share of random-entry draws that **beat** the RWI timer | **90%** (total return), **95%** (Sharpe) |

A random selection of days with the *same* invested fraction and the *same* turnover profile
outperforms the actual RWI-timed book on total return in 9 of 10 draws and on Sharpe in 19 of 20.
The flag is not merely uninformative — it is actively worse than picking entry days at random.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic two-regime (trend/chop) Markov world, both regimes sharing the same daily shock
scale so a naive volatility read can't tell them apart — only sustained directional displacement
can (which is exactly what the RWI is built to catch). `edge = 0` is the null: both regimes carry
the same expected drift.

| world | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|
| null (edge = 0), **20 seeds** | mean **−0.03** (sd 1.09), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 1/20 seeds** |
| planted edge = +0.006/day in the trend regime (seed 678) | **+9.54** (hit rate 64.6%) |

The 1/20 null crossings are consistent with the ~5% nominal false-positive rate of a two-sided
*t* = 2 threshold — the detector is properly calibrated, not biased — and a genuinely
trend-persistent world with a real (if generously sized) planted drift edge lights it up hard.
*(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** RWI-high > 1 fires on 56.8% of SPY sessions (already a weak "rare event"
  claim) and does **not** predict a better next-session return: SPY alone is directionally
  backwards at *t* = −1.64, and pooled across five liquid instruments the wrong-signed gap
  *clears* the bar (Welch *t* = **−2.16**) — a small, real headwind, not the promised edge. A
  matched-count random-day placebo beats the flag's own mean 96% of the time.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The RWI-high long timer returns +81.8% gross over 21.5 years against
  buy & hold's +831.3% (Sharpe 0.30 vs 0.64), and turns net-negative at 10 bps one-way costs. A
  block-shuffled, exposure- and turnover-matched random-entry control **beats the real timer in
  90% of draws by total return and 95% by Sharpe.**
- **"Beats a coin?" — BUSTED.** A same-exposure random-entry coin flip outperforms the RWI-timed
  book on both total return and Sharpe in the large majority of draws — the "statistically
  non-random" trigger does not even clear the bar of picking days at random.
